title: His views on integration and race
summary: She discusses their mixed marriage, his support for integration, his reaction to riots, his having to enter clubs by the back way, and his Indian ancestry.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did George ever talk about integration and color children?

Yes. We spoke with him quite a bit. George is a very honest person, and he was very honest and open with me especially. Naturally, both being different colors. We both knew the burden we had to face with the population and so forth. And he naturally was all for integration. He was schooled in an integrated school his early years. He couldn't understand the riots that are going on now. He says that the people were bringing it upon themselves, both races. Not one, but the other, both races. He was very frank with me. I mean, we'd joke about it because I'd always, he'd always say, he'd tan my height if I was naughty. And I'd tell him if he wasn't good, I'd tan him until he turned white. I mean, it was just a pass on joke. Yeah. Now, when he was with other people, he was very polite, very well-mannered. He wouldn't say a word. Sometimes they would hurt him in their remarks. But he was going to bite his tongue and hold back. And. And.

He was a very honest, forthright person. If he liked the person, he couldn't do enough for him. If he didn't, he would either keep clear out of the way or you would know it, one way or another. He wasn't one to, like they say, pussyfoot around. He used to hurt him so many times going to the clubs and he'd have to walk in the back way. Because I know many times after I arrived, if he played in one or two hotels or something, he said it wasn't long before this, he said I'd have to go in the back way. He said, well we've been walking together now. And if we'd walk into a restaurant to eat, it worried him somewhat. Because he was a fighter and if anybody made an unkind word in any way, he was ready. I'd sometimes have to control him rather than start something. But he says, no, nobody's going to say anything one way or another. He's got to let me know. So as far as integration goes, or the color part of it, he treated people as they treated him, regardless of color. Color was no problem to him unless they caused it. And naturally being part Indian. He had some of that Indian blood in him. He didn't like anybody talking about the Indians either because his great grandmother was Indian. So with George, as far as the color went, he loved all people of all races. If they treated him properly, he treated them. In return, I know my little, my daughter, he just loves her. I mean, he's a little guy like Mary. He said, as far as the white race went. Or Bobo. When Bobo came here. Lord, that child used to climb up on his bed all the time, hug him and kiss him and so forth. And he was so proud when I entered him into the school with David and Graham, his grandchildren. He was the first little white boy to enter that school. And he was tickle-pain. George was happy when I enrolled him in that school.
